subject: Model decision making help: gdistsamp versus pointcountOpen for line-transect surveys

messages.author: 5e772dd7993d30c1
messages.subject: Model decision making help: gdistsamp versus pointcountOpen for line-transect surveys
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm a MSc student working on a project where I'm determining avian abundance on cover crop fields versus fields with no cover crops during wintering, migration, and breeding seasons. I had my first run this past season but unfortunately due to covid, I had to cut my season short and only obtained wintering bird data.

We are to conduct 2 replicates each season and have approximately 80 cover crop fields and 20 control fields. Each field has two 100-m line-transects. Birds were counted if they were heard and/or observed and their distances and bearing from the line were taken. Right now, I have not decided how I am going to bin my distances, but many of my species detected were placed in a >100 category (these species were 99% of the time forest obligate species that would not be using these fields so will not be included in the data analysis). Vegetation data was also collected on the fields, mostly for vegetative height, cover, and species present, and will act as my covariate. Time, temperature, and weather conditions were also taken.

While I am familiar with R, I am still trying to bolster my stats abilities and truthfully am unsure of how to approach this analysis. I'm using the data that I collected now as a way to learn and improve my study design as well as learn how to properly do my future analyses. My main question is whether or not I should be using gdistsamp or pointcountOpen for this project. I am also quite confused on what may seem as a simple question: I am unsure, if I were to go with gdistsamp, of what the phiformula means and how to truly calculate availability since these species are moving constantly from place to place.

Any and all help/insight/advice is greatly appreciated!

Thank you!

Brittany

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Model decision making help: gdistsamp versus pointcountOpen for line-transect surveys
parts:
Hi,

 Seems like it would be worth using some sort of distance sampling model if that information is available and you trust it--note that both a gdistsamp and distsampOpen could work (papers at doi.org/10.1890/10-2433.1 for gdistsamp; and doi.org/10.1890/14-1625.1). The difference between the two relate to dynamics parameters that describe how N's in time 1 relate to the N's in time 2. Of the two, I'd probably use gdistsamp with the data in hand, but you'd want to have some more formal justification for choosing one.  

I'm sure somebody else can give the phiformula question a better response than I can at this moment (and the parameter is explained well in the describing paper, so again, definitely give that a read), but maybe here's a very coarse description. If you visit some soy field on monday and then again on wednesday, some of the birds in the field on the first visit may not be in the field on the second visit (or vice versa). The gist is that some of the variation between monday and wednesday's counts relate to detection (informed by the distribution of observed distances across monday and wednesday and perhaps substantial changes in the distribution of observed distances between monday and wednesday), and some of the variation relates to how many birds were actually sitting in the field (or sitting in the field and singing) on monday vs. wednesday. The phi formula is used to specify whether one thinks the number of birds that could be detected--because they are sitting in the field, or sitting in the field and singing--when the field is visited has some constant average value, or whether that average changes based on, say, whether it is raining or not, etc.


John

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Model decision making help: gdistsamp versus pointcountOpen for line-transect surveys
parts:
Ok, follow-up. This is a tough place for broad questions about how to analyze the data--pry better for specific coding or formatting questions--just because these questions take a lot of energy to answer and because online boards are probably not a great venue for teaching. That said, here's the best quick description of the models I can give, and hopefully you can work out a plan of attack with advisor, committee member, etc. 

[for data formatting, etc., https://www.montana.edu/screel/teaching/bioe-440r-521/bioe-440-distance-sampling.html and https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/distsamp.pdf provide good overviews--and there are pry others if you search around on google.]

The three distance sampling options in unmarked are distsamp, gdistsamp, distsampOpen:

1) The closed distance sampling model (distsamp) estimates parameters that describe the expected abundance (lambda) and probability of detecting a given bird (sigma, via pformula). All parameters here and elsewhere could be estimated as varying in relation to covariates. Typically, distsamp is used to analyze data at a number of sites only visited once.With the data you have now, you could fit one of these models by 'stacking' the data (structuring the data so that each site*visit is treated as a different 'site', and adding a covariate for visit and/or year). This ignores any correlation between counts during different visits to the same site), and so to properly report the uncertainty may require some tricks after the fact (namely, a non parametric bootstrap). Ideally, average density = lambda/area. However, if some birds are not available for detection for behavioral reasons (see below), then this is really the density of 'available' birds. The formatting here for your y data as of now would be nsites*2 rows, and ndistance bins columns.

2) gdistsamp fits a model that estimates parameters associated with the expected number of birds that might have been available for detection (lambda), the probability that each bird that might have been available to detect was available to detect during time/visit t (phi), and the probability that any available bird was detected (sigma). Lack of availability might relate to not being physically present at a site during a given time, or might relate to a bird behaving such that it is essentially undetectable. If lack of availability is exclusively related to not being physically present, average density = lambda*phi/area. If lack of availability is exclusively related to behavior, average density = lambda/area (unmarked can report this, but note that it may not be appropriate).Typically this model is used to analyze data at a number of sites that have been visited a few times during, say, the same year. As the total duration across the visits increases, lambda becomes a little more difficult to interpret biologically. The formatting here for your y data as of now would be nsites rows, and ndistance bins*2 columns--each new visit adds another ndistance bin columns.

3) distsampOpen fits a model that estimates parameters that describe the expected abundance (lambda) during time 1,  the probability of detecting a bird, and parameters that describe the *change* from N[i, t] to N[i, t+1]. Typically this model is used to analyze data at sites that have been visited once per time period (e.g., once a year; although varying intervals could potentially work), when one is interested in population dynamics (the parameters associated with a density-independent or density-dependent model for population growth, demographic parameters related to the number of animals that 'stay' in a site from t to t+1 and the number of animals that newly 'arrive' at a site in t+1). The formatting here for your y data as or now would be nsites rows, and ndistance bins*2 columns--each new visit adds another ndistance bin columns.

'distsamp' is the most direct and simplest way to model 'just abundance'. It will be biased (as an estimator of actual abundance) if not all animals are available, and this motivated the development of the model underlying 'gdistsamp'. 'gdistsamp' will--*I think*--produce biased estimates of density if availability relates to both movement and behavior, and if individuals die or are recruited during the survey, gdistsamp is not robust to that, either (for multiple years, it might make sense to stack the data in so that a site is really a site*year). So really the choice depends upon what assumptions you think are reasonable, what you are trying to estimate, how you are willing to interpret it. 

Your design is complicated. A big question is what constitutes a site. I don't know how to answer this because I have no idea how close the transects within the same field are, whether they are surveyed on the same day, etc. Are birds moving from transect to transect? If you survey both transect on a field on the same day or even exactly concurrently, could birds end up counted in both transect? I'd actually focus first on trying to figure out what defines a site, and then consider what design allows you to estimate the things of interest with the least headache. Three things to keep in mind. 1) dealing with the nesting here using random effects isn't possible in unmarked. 2) if you use the same design next year, it's also not possible to fit a model that estimates both availability and dynamics parameters in unmarked. If you used the same design next year, some sort of stacking seems necessary for either gdistamp (site by year ='site') or distsamp (site by year by visit ='site') to make much sense. 3) Although nobody likes doing it, very worst case scenario, a complicated design can always be simplified by throwing some data away (or better, with-holding some for out of sample model evaluation!). You could (for example) always sub-sample one transect and visit within each field and fit a model using, say, distsamp. You could fit the same model 4 times (one for each transect*visit replicate in a field) and, for peace of mind, check to see if the results are relatively stable, or if there's some pattern across time or transect that might inform how you sample next year. 

John
